questions.title: Confused by the procedural history: What is the current status of the district court's injunctions?
questions.question_body: I'm trying to track the procedural posture of Pacito v. Trump. The court says it 'vacates' previous administrative stays from July and March, but then says the district court's February and March injunctions are 'stayed in their entirety' except for a specific part. Does this mean the district court's rulings are currently inactive, or did the vacating of the previous stays put them back in effect briefly before the new stay was issued? I'm struggling to understand the net effect on the parties.

questions.title: How does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) interact with the Refugee Act of 1980?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs argue that Executive Order 14163 violates the Refugee Act of 1980. However, the court relies heavily on Trump v. Hawaii and 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) to say the President has 'ample power' to suspend entry. If the Refugee Act establishes a 'general rule' for treating refugees, how can § 1182(f) allow the President to essentially suspend the entire program? Does the specific authority in § 1182(f) override the general mandates of the Refugee Act?

questions.title: Mandatory vs. Permissive: How to reconcile 'shall' with 'authorized' in 8 U.S.C. § 1522?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the split between the majority and Judge Lee. The majority points to the word 'shall' in § 1522(a) to argue that the government has a mandatory duty to provide resettlement services. Judge Lee, however, argues that because the section title uses the word 'Authorization' and other subsections say the Director is 'authorized,' the whole thing is permissive. In statutory interpretation, which carries more weight: the title of a section or the use of the word 'shall' in a specific subsection?

questions.title: What is the legal significance of the government's 'uncertainty' regarding new agencies?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that the government told the district court it was preparing a 'request for proposals' for new resettlement agencies, but later admitted it didn't know if any progress had been made. The court then uses this 'uncertainty' as a reason to force the government to reinstate the old cooperative agreements. Is this a specific legal standard under the APA, or is the court just using the facts to justify an equitable remedy?

questions.title: Does the 'limited carveout' for conditionally approved refugees still exist?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions a 'limited carveout' from a previous stay that applied to individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before January 20, 2025. Then, in the discussion section, it says the district court's orders are stayed 'in their entirety, except as noted below.' The 'noted below' section focuses on the § 1522 resettlement services. Does this mean the previous carveout for conditionally approved refugees was wiped out by this new order, or is it subsumed into the services requirement?
